title: The Third Phase: Calling unto Islam beyond Makkah
arabicTitle: المرحلة الثالثة: الدعوة إلى الإسلام خارج مكة

topics.title: Islam being introduced to Arabian Tribes and Individuals

paragraphs.text: In Shawwal (in the last of May or the beginning of June 619 A.D.), ten years after receiving his mission from his Lord, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) set out towards At-Ta'if, about 60 kilometres from Makkah, in the company of his freed slave Zaid bin Haritha, inviting people to Islam. But contrary to his expectations, the general atmosphere was terribly hostile. He approached the family of 'Umair, who were reckoned amongst the nobility of the town, but all of them turned a deaf ear to his message and used abusive language. Three brothers from the chieftains of Thaqeef — 'Abd Yaleel, Mas'ud and Habeeb, sons of 'Amr bin 'Umair Ath-Thaqafy — met the Prophet (Peace be upon him), who invited them to embrace Islam, but they impudently jeered at him. One said: "He is tearing the cloths of Al-Ka'bah; is it true that Allah has sent you as a Messenger?" The second said: "Has Allah not found someone else to entrust with His Message?" The third said: "I swear by Allah that I will never have any contact with you. If you are really the Messenger of Allah, then you are too serious to retort back; and if you are belying Allah, then it is imperative not to speak to you." The Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him), finding them hopeless cases, stood up and left saying: "Should you indulge in these practices of yours, never divulge them to me."

For ten days he stayed there delivering his message to several people, one after another, but all to no purpose. Stirred up to hasten the departure of the unwelcome visitor, the people hooted him through the alley-ways, pelted him with stones and obliged him to flee from the city, pursued by a relentless rabble. Blood flowed down both his legs; and Zaid, endeavouring to shield him, was wounded in the head. The mob did not desist until they had chased him two or three miles across the sandy plains to the foot of the surrounding hills. There, wearied and exhausted, he took refuge in one of the orchards, and rested against the wall of a vineyard.

At a time when the whole world seemed to have turned against him, Muhammad (Peace be upon him) turned to his Lord and betook himself to prayer. The following touching words are still preserved as those through which his oppressed soul gave vent to its distress: "O Allah! To You alone I make complaint of my helplessness, the paucity of my resources and my insignificance before mankind. You are the most Merciful of the mercifuls. You are the Lord of the helpless and the weak, O Lord of mine! Into whose hands would You abandon me: into the hands of an unsympathetic distant relative who would sullenly frown at me, or to the enemy who has been given control over my affairs? But if Your wrath does not fall on me, there is nothing for me to worry about."

"I seek protection in the light of Your Countenance, which illuminates the heavens and dispels darkness, and which controls all affairs in this world as well as in the Hereafter. May it never be that I should incur Your wrath, or that You should be wrathful to me. And there is no power nor resource, but Yours alone."

Seeing him in this helpless situation, Rabi'a's two sons, wealthy Makkans, were moved on grounds of kinship and compassion, and sent to him one of their Christian servants with a tray of grapes. The Prophet (Peace be upon him) accepted the fruit with the pious invocation: "In the Name of Allah." The Christian servant 'Addas was greatly impressed by these words and said: "These are words which people in this land do not generally use." The Prophet (Peace be upon him) inquired whence he came and what religion he professed. 'Addas replied: "I am a Christian by faith and come from Nineveh." The Prophet (Peace be upon him) said: "You belong to the city of the righteous Jonah, son of Matta." 'Addas asked anxiously if he knew anything about Jonah. The Prophet (Peace be upon him) remarked: "He is my brother. He was a Prophet and so am I." Thereupon 'Addas paid homage to Muhammad (Peace be upon him) and kissed his hands. His masters admonished him, but he replied: "None on the earth is better than he is. He has revealed to me a truth which only a Prophet can do."

Heart-broken and depressed, Muhammad (Peace be upon him) set out on the way back to Makkah. When he reached Qarn Al-Manazil, Allah, the Almighty, sent him Gabriel together with the angel of mountains. The latter asked the Prophet (Peace be upon him) for permission to bury Makkah between Al-Akhshabain — Abu Qubais and Qu'ayqa'an mountains. Full narration of this event was given by 'Aishah (May Allah be pleased with her): "I asked the Prophet (Peace be upon him) if he had ever experienced a worse day than Uhud. He answered that he had suffered a lot from those people, but the most painful was on the day of 'Aqabah. I went seeking support from Ibn 'Abd Yalil bin 'Abd Kalal, but he spurned me. I set out wearied and grieved until I suddenly realized I was in Qarn Ath-Tha'alib. There, I looked up and saw a cloud casting its shade on me, and Gabriel addressing me: 'Allah has heard your people's words and sent you the angel of mountains to your aid.' The latter gave me his greetings and asked for my permission to bury Makkah between Al-Akhshabain. I said in reply that I would rather have someone from their loins who will worship Allah, the All-Mighty, with no associate."

The Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him) then proceeded to Wadi Nakhlah where he stayed for a few days. During his stay there, Allah sent him a company of jinns who listened to him reciting the Noble Qur'ân: "And (remember) when We sent towards you [Muhammad (Peace be upon him)] Nafran (three to ten persons) of the jinns, (quietly) listening to the Qur'ân. When they stood in the presence thereof, they said: 'Listen in silence!' And when it was finished, they returned to their people, as warners. They said: 'O our people! Verily! We have heard a Book (this Qur'ân) sent down after Moses, confirming what came before it, it guides to the Truth and to a Straight Path. O our people! Respond to Allah's Caller and believe in him. He (Allah) will forgive you of your sins, and will save you from a painful torment.'" [46:29-31] The same incident is referred to in Sûrah Al-Jinn: "Say [O Muhammad (Peace be upon him)]: 'It has been revealed to me that a group of jinns listened (to this Qur'ân). They said: Verily! We have heard a wonderful Recital! It guides to the Right Path, and we have believed therein, and we shall never join (in worship) anything with our Lord (Allah).'" [72:1,2]

From the context of these verses we can establish that the Prophet (Peace be upon him) was not aware of the presence of that group of jinns; it was only when Allah revealed those verses that he came to know of it, and it was the first time they came, though they repeated their visits later on. The presence of that company of jinns comes in the context of the Divine support given to His Messenger, and constitutes a propitious sign of ultimate victory for the Call of Islam, providing an unshakable proof that no power, however mighty, could alter what is wrought by Allah: "And whosoever does not respond to Allah's Caller, he cannot escape on earth, and there will be no Auliyâ (protectors) besides Allah. Those are in manifest error." [46:32] "And we think that we cannot escape (from the punishment of) Allah in the earth, nor can we escape (from the punishment) by flight." [72:12]

Given this support and auspicious start, the depression and sadness that had beset him since he was driven out of At-Ta'if lifted, and he turned his face towards Makkah with fresh determination. Zaid bin Harithah said to him, "How dare you step into Makkah after they (Quraish) have expatriated you?" The Prophet (Peace be upon him) answered: "Hearken Zaid, Allah will surely provide relief and He will verily support His religion and Prophet." When he was a short distance from Makkah, he retired to Hira' Cave, whence he despatched a man from Khuza'ah tribe to Al-Akhnas bin Shuraiq seeking his protection. The latter said he was Quraish's ally and in no position to offer protection. He despatched the messenger to Suhail bin 'Amr, but to no avail. Al-Mut'im bin 'Adi, a notable in Makkah, however, volunteered. He asked his people to prepare themselves fully armed and then asked Muhammad (Peace be upon him) to enter the town and the Holy Sanctuary. The Prophet (Peace be upon him) observed a two-Rak'a prayer and left for his house guarded by the heavily-armed 'Adi's.

It has been reported that later Abu Jahl asked Mut'im if his behaviour suggested protection or conversion; the latter replied it was merely protection, and Abu Jahl was relieved. The Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him) never forgot Mut'im's favour. At the conclusion of the battle of Badr, he declared publicly that if Mut'im had been still alive and asked for the release of the Quraishite captives, he would not deny him his request. In Dhul Qa'dah, the tenth year of Prophethood (July 619), the Prophet (Peace be upon him) returned to Makkah to resume his activities. The time for pilgrimage was approaching, so he hastened to introduce both tribes and individuals to Islam and call upon them to embrace it, just as had been his practice since the fourth year of his Prophethood.

On the authority of Az-Zuhri, of the tribes that Islam was introduced to, we could speak of Banu 'Amir bin Sa'sa'ah, Muharib bin Khasfa, Fazarah, Ghassan, Murrah, Haneefah, Saleem, 'Abs, Banu Nasr, Banu Al-Buka', Kindah, Kalb, Al-Harith bin Ka'b, Udhrah and the people of Hadramout. Islam was not introduced to them in one single year but rather repeatedly, from the fourth year till the last pre-migration season of pilgrimage. They however remained obdurate and none of them responded positively.

He visited a sept of Banu Kalb known as Banu 'Abdullah, called them to Allah's Message and entreated them to accept it for the sake of Allah Who had chosen a beautiful name for their father, but without avail. He called on Bani Haneefah in their habitation, but received very repugnant treatment. He addressed Bani 'Amir bin Sa'sa'ah, calling them to abandon idolatry. One of them, Buhairah bin Firras, answered: "Should we give you allegiance and Allah give you power over your opponents, will you give us the right to inheritance and succeed you in power?" The Prophet replied: "The whole affair lies in Allah's Hands. He gives the power to whomever He desires." The man commented: "Do you expect us to incur the wrath of the Arabs without the least hope of leadership? We can readily dispense with your offers."

When Banu 'Amir returned to their habitations, they narrated the story to an elderly man who had lingered behind because he was too old. They told him, "A young man of Quraish of Bani 'Abdul Muttalib, claiming that he is a Prophet, contacted us and invited us to embrace his religion." The old sheikh was struck by the news and swore: "He is really Ishmaelite. He is the Truth. How did it happen that you misjudged his words?"

The Prophet (Peace be upon him) was not dismayed. He persisted in his mission and did not confine his efforts to tribes but also conducted contacts with individuals, from some of whom he received a favourable response. Among the early converts was Swaid bin Samit, an intelligent, discreet poet from Yathrib. During his stay in Makkah for pilgrimage, he encountered the Prophet (Peace be upon him), who invited him to Islam. Swaid imparted to him some of Luqman's wisdom; the Prophet approved of it but told the man he had something far better, and recited some verses from the Qur'ân. The words appealed to his pure nature and he accepted Islam at once. He was killed in the battle of Bu'ath, in the eleventh year of Prophethood.

Another was Eyas bin Mu'adh, a youth from the Aws tribe who came as a member of a delegation seeking alliance with Quraish against the rival Khazraj. The Prophet (Peace be upon him) advised them to follow a better course, introduced Islam, and recited some verses. Eyas's heart immediately absorbed the Divine Message. Abul Haisar Anas bin Rafi', a member of the delegation, disapproved and silenced the boy by hurling dust into his face. The people then left Madinah, having failed to establish an alliance. Shortly after arrival, the boy breathed his last acclaiming Allah's Name.

Abu Dhar Al-Ghifari used to live in the suburbs of Yathrib. News of the Islamization of Swaid and Eyas reached him and constituted a turning point in his life. He sent his brother to Makkah for details, then went himself, and after some difficulty managed to meet the Prophet (Peace be upon him). No sooner was he exposed to the real nature of Islam than he embraced it. Despite the Prophet's plea not to divulge his move, Abu Dhar went directly to the Holy Sanctuary and publicly declared his testimony. The heathens hurried and beat him almost to death, until Al-'Abbas intervened, warning against killing someone whose tribe controlled the strategic commercial caravan routes to Makkah. The event recurred the following morning, with Al-'Abbas again coming to his rescue.

Tufail bin 'Amr Ad-Dausi was an honest poet and chief of the Ad-Daus tribe, inhabiting an area close to Yemen. He arrived in Makkah in the eleventh year of Prophethood. The Makkans warned him against listening to the Prophet (Peace be upon him), so he even stuffed his ears with cotton. However, when he entered the mosque and saw Muhammad (Peace be upon him) praying, out of curiosity he approached and heard his appealing words. He followed the Prophet (Peace be upon him) into his house and heard some verses of the Qur'ân; he embraced Islam and testified to the faith. He asked the Prophet (Peace be upon him) for a supportive sign to ease his task — and was given a Divinely bestowed light in his whip. He called his father and wife, who responded, and then his people; he and seventy or eighty of his followers emigrated to Madinah after the Trench Battle. He was a perfect fighter in the cause of Allah and was martyred in the Al-Yamama events.

Dhumad Al-Azdi came from Azd Shanu'a in Yemen, a specialist in incantation. He arrived in Makkah to hear the fools there say that Muhammad (Peace be upon him) was out of his mind, and decided to practise his craft on the Prophet (Peace be upon him), who on seeing him said: "Praise is to Allah, we entertain His praise and seek His help. Whomsoever Allah guides, none will lead astray, and whomsoever Allah leads astray, none will guide. I testify there is no god but Allah and Muhammad is His servant and Messenger." Dhumad requested the Prophet (Peace be upon him) to echo the words again, and was granted his wish thrice. He then said: "I have heard the soothsayers, sorcerers and poets, but never have I experienced the sweetness of your words," and gave a pledge of a sincere convert.

topics.topicSummary: In the tenth year, the Prophet ﷺ went to At-Ta'if with Zaid bin Haritha but was rejected, mocked and stoned until he bled. In a vineyard he made his famous supplication of helplessness; the Christian servant 'Addas believed, and on the way back the angel of mountains offered to crush the town — which he refused, hoping for righteous descendants. A company of jinns embraced his recitation [46:29-31; 72:1-2]. He re-entered Makkah under Al-Mut'im bin 'Adi's protection and resumed introducing Islam to many tribes (who all refused) and to individuals — Swaid, Eyas, Abu Dhar, Tufail Ad-Dausi and Dhumad — who believed.

In a vineyard he made his famous supplication complaining only to Allah of his helplessness

A company of jinns listened to the Qur'an and believed [46:29-31; 72:1-2]
He re-entered Makkah under the protection of Al-Mut'im bin 'Adi, whose favour he never forgot (recalled after Badr)

quiz.answer: He refused, hoping their descendants would worship Allah alone

topics.title: Hope inspiring Breezes from the Madinese

paragraphs.text: It was during the pilgrimage season, in the eleventh year of Prophethood, that the Islamic Call found the righteous seeds through which it would grow into tall trees whose leaves would foster the new faith and shelter the new converts from the injustices of Quraish. It was the Prophet's wise practice to meet the delegates of the Arabian tribes by night so that the hostile Makkans would not debar him. In the company of his two truthful Companions 'Ali and Abu Bakr, he had a talk regarding Islam with Bani Dhuhal, but they suspended their conversion. In pursuit of the same objective, the Prophet and his Companions passed by 'Aqabat Mina, where they encountered six men from Yathrib, all of whom from the Khazraj tribe: As'ad bin Zurarah, 'Awf bin Harith, Rafi' bin Malik, Qutbah bin 'Amir, 'Uqbah bin 'Amir and Jabir bin 'Abdullah.

The Madinese always heard the Jews say that a Prophet was about to rise, for the time for a new dispensation had arrived; him they would follow and then smite their enemies as the children of 'Ad and Iram had been smitten.

"Of what tribe are you?" asked the Prophet. "Of the tribe of Khazraj," they replied. "Are you the allies of the Jews?" the Prophet enquired. They said: "Yes." "Then why not sit down for a little and I will speak to you?" The offer was readily accepted, for the fame of Muhammad (Peace be upon him) had spread to Madinah and the strangers were curious to see the man who had created a stir in the whole area. The Prophet (Peace be upon him) presented to them an exposé of Islam, explained its implications and the responsibilities that fell upon those who accepted it.

When the Prophet (Peace be upon him) concluded his talk, they said among themselves: "Know surely, this is the Prophet with whom the Jews are ever threatening us; wherefore let us make haste and be the first to join him." They therefore embraced Islam, and said to the Prophet: "We have left our community, for no tribe is so divided by hatred and rancour as they are. Allah may cement our ties through you. So let us go and invite them to this religion of yours; and if Allah unites them in it, no man will be dearer than you."

The handful of Madinese converts remained steady to the cause, and they preached Islam with full zeal and devotion, with the result that they succeeded in winning adherents from amongst their fellow citizens; hardly was there a house in Madinah not talking curiously and enthusiastically about the Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him).

topics.topicSummary: During the pilgrimage of the eleventh year, the Prophet ﷺ met six men of the Khazraj from Yathrib at 'Aqabat Mina. Having long heard the Jews foretell a coming Prophet, they recognized him, embraced Islam, and resolved to be the first to invite their own feud-torn people. On returning to Madinah they preached so zealously that scarcely a house remained that was not discussing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
keyPoints: In the eleventh year of Prophethood, the Call found fertile ground among the people of Yathrib (Madinah)
The Prophet ﷺ met delegates by night to avoid the hostile Makkans, accompanied by 'Ali and Abu Bakr

quiz.question: From which city were the six men whom the Prophet ﷺ met at 'Aqabat Mina?
Why were the men of Yathrib quick to recognize the Prophet ﷺ?
options: They had met him before in Makkah

quiz.answer: The Jews among them had long foretold that a Prophet was about to rise

topics.title: Marriage of the Prophet [pbuh] to 'Aishah [R]

paragraphs.text: In Shawwal of the same year, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) concluded a marriage contract with 'Aishah (May Allah be pleased with her), 'the truth verifier', when she was six of age, and consummated his marriage with her in Shawwal, the year 1 A.H. in Madinah, when she was nine.

topics.topicSummary: In Shawwal of the same year, the Prophet ﷺ concluded the marriage contract with 'Aishah (RA), and the marriage was consummated in Shawwal of 1 A.H. in Madinah.
keyPoints: The Prophet ﷺ concluded the marriage contract with 'Aishah (RA) in Shawwal of that year
The marriage was consummated in Shawwal of the year 1 A.H. in Madinah
